claim: Pancreatic islets are innervated by autonomic and sensory nerves that influence their function.
source: Pancreatic islets are innervated by autonomic and sensory nerves that influence their function.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature (Taborsky et al., 1998; Havel and Ahren, 1997; Ahrén, 2000; Gilliam et al., 2007) as indicated in the full text.

claim: Neural crest cells are in close contact with endocrine cells early in development.
source: Neural crest cells are in close contact with endocrine cells early in development.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations from live imaging and immunostaining data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Neural crest-derived cells give rise to neurons that extend axons toward the islet as they migrate away.
source: We find these cells give rise to neurons that extend axons toward the islet as they surprisingly migrate away.
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data and lineage tracing experiments shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Specific ablation of neurons that detach from the islet partly prevents other neurons from migrating away from the islet resulting in diminished innervation.
source: Specific ablation of these neurons partly prevents other neurons from migrating away from the islet resulting in diminished innervation.
evidence: This claim is supported by two-photon laser ablation experiments and quantification of innervation density shown in Figure 6.

claim: Neurons establish connections with their targets before migrating away, representing a novel mode of innervation.
source: Thus, our studies establish the zebrafish as a model to interrogate mechanisms of organ innervation, and reveal a novel mode of innervation whereby neurons establish connections with their targets before migrating away.
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data showing the sequence of cellular events during innervation.

claim: Studies have highlighted the role of autonomic innervation on pancreas development and endocrine hormone secretion.
source: Studies have highlighted the role of autonomic innervation on pancreas development and endocrine hormone secretion (Ahrén, 2000; Borden et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Whether innervation directly modulates glucose homeostasis and contributes to diabetes progression remains controversial.
source: Whether innervation directly modulates glucose homeostasis and contributes to diabetes progression remains controversial, despite effects of sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves on pancreatic islet hormone secretion (Ahrén, 2000; Gautam et al., 2006) and the role of sensory fibers on autoimmunity (Tsui et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and represents a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: Differences in autonomic innervation pattern in the endocrine pancreas have been observed between rodents and humans.
source: Although differences in autonomic innervation pattern in the endocrine pancreas have been observed between rodents and humans (Rodriguez-Diaz et al., 2011, 2012), the influence of the autonomic nervous system on pancreatic hormone secretion is conserved across species (Havel and Ahren, 1997; Ahrén, 2000; Gilliam et al., 2007; Borden et al., 2013; Gautam et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The influence of the autonomic nervous system on pancreatic hormone secretion is conserved across species.
source: Although differences in autonomic innervation pattern in the endocrine pancreas have been observed between rodents and humans (Rodriguez-Diaz et al., 2011, 2012), the influence of the autonomic nervous system on pancreatic hormone secretion is conserved across species (Havel and Ahren, 1997; Ahrén, 2000; Gilliam et al., 2007; Borden et al., 2013; Gautam et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The difference in innervation pattern between rodents and humans has been challenged by immunostaining of thick tissue sections and whole mounts.
source: More recently, this difference in pattern has been challenged by immunostaining of thick tissue sections and whole mounts (Hsueh et al., 2017; Tang et al., 2018, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Higher innervation density is observed in human fetal pancreas in comparison to adult.
source: Indeed, higher innervation density is observed in human fetal pancreas in comparison to adult (Proshchina et al., 2014), and loss of innervation is observed in humans with Type one diabetes (Mundinger et al., 2016), as it is in several rodent models of autoimmune diabetes (Mundinger and Taborsky, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Loss of innervation is observed in humans with Type one diabetes.
source: Indeed, higher innervation density is observed in human fetal pancreas in comparison to adult (Proshchina et al., 2014), and loss of innervation is observed in humans with Type one diabetes (Mundinger et al., 2016), as it is in several rodent models of autoimmune diabetes (Mundinger and Taborsky, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Loss of innervation is observed in several rodent models of autoimmune diabetes.
source: Indeed, higher innervation density is observed in human fetal pancreas in comparison to adult (Proshchina et al., 2014), and loss of innervation is observed in humans with Type one diabetes (Mundinger et al., 2016), as it is in several rodent models of autoimmune diabetes (Mundinger and Taborsky, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Whether innervation is a result of vasculature-derived guidance cues remains controversial.
source: Whether innervation is a result of vasculature- (Reinert et al., 2014; Cabrera-Vásquez et al., 2009) or neural crest- (Plank et al., 2011; Nekrep et al., 2008; Muñoz-Bravo et al., 2013; Kozlova and Jansson, 2009; Jiang et al., 2003; Young and Newgreen, 2001; Arntfield and van der Kooy, 2013) derived guidance cues remains controversial.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature representing different viewpoints.

claim: Whether innervation is a result of neural crest-derived guidance cues remains controversial.
source: Whether innervation is a result of vasculature- (Reinert et al., 2014; Cabrera-Vásquez et al., 2009) or neural crest- (Plank et al., 2011; Nekrep et al., 2008; Muñoz-Bravo et al., 2013; Kozlova and Jansson, 2009; Jiang et al., 2003; Young and Newgreen, 2001; Arntfield and van der Kooy, 2013) derived guidance cues remains controversial.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature representing different viewpoints.

claim: Lineage tracing and knockout studies have suggested a neural crest origin for pancreatic nerves.
source: And although lineage tracing and knockout studies have suggested a neural crest origin for pancreatic nerves (Plank et al., 2011), interpretations can be limited by the Cre driver line specificity (Chen et al., 2017; Lewis et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Interpretations of lineage tracing studies can be limited by the Cre driver line specificity.
source: And although lineage tracing and knockout studies have suggested a neural crest origin for pancreatic nerves (Plank et al., 2011), interpretations can be limited by the Cre driver line specificity (Chen et al., 2017; Lewis et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: It remains difficult to differentiate between the local effects of autonomic fibers on islet cell physiology from the simultaneous influence on other organs that can indirectly modulate hormone secretion.
source: Additionally, it remains difficult to differentiate between the local effects of autonomic fibers on islet cell physiology from the simultaneous influence on other organs that can indirectly modulate hormone secretion (Taborsky, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The zebrafish has organs homologous to mammalian ones and conserved signaling and metabolic pathways.
source: The zebrafish, with organs homologous to mammalian ones and conserved signaling and metabolic pathways (Schlegel and Stainier, 2007; Seth et al., 2013; Ober et al., 2003), is ideal to study the role of neuronal innervation during endocrine pancreas development.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The zebrafish is ideal to study the role of neuronal innervation during endocrine pancreas development.
source: The zebrafish, with organs homologous to mammalian ones and conserved signaling and metabolic pathways (Schlegel and Stainier, 2007; Seth et al., 2013; Ober et al., 2003), is ideal to study the role of neuronal innervation during endocrine pancreas development.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and the rationale for using zebrafish as a model.

claim: The transparency and rapid embryogenesis of zebrafish allow for the study of developmental processes with single-cell resolution using in vivo time-lapse imaging.
source: The transparency and rapid embryogenesis of zebrafish, together with fluorescent reporters, allow for the study of developmental processes with single-cell resolution using in vivo time-lapse imaging (Beis and Stainier, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature and is established knowledge about zebrafish as a model organism.

claim: The onset of pancreatic innervation in zebrafish arises early in development.
source: We found that the onset of pancreatic innervation arises early in development (Figure 1A–D), preceding the fusion of the dorsal and ventral pancreatic buds (Field et al., 2003), and that prior to 120 hpf, the majority of this innervation is derived from the vagus nerve (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A-D.

claim: Pancreatic innervation in zebrafish precedes the fusion of the dorsal and ventral pancreatic buds.
source: We found that the onset of pancreatic innervation arises early in development (Figure 1A–D), preceding the fusion of the dorsal and ventral pancreatic buds (Field et al., 2003), and that prior to 120 hpf, the majority of this innervation is derived from the vagus nerve (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A-D and a citation to prior literature about pancreatic bud fusion.

claim: Prior to 120 hpf, the majority of pancreatic innervation is derived from the vagus nerve.
source: We found that the onset of pancreatic innervation arises early in development (Figure 1A–D), preceding the fusion of the dorsal and ventral pancreatic buds (Field et al., 2003), and that prior to 120 hpf, the majority of this innervation is derived from the vagus nerve (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Migration of the vagus nerve near the pancreatic islet was first observed at 50 hpf.
source: Looking more closely, we first observed the migration of the vagus nerve near the pancreatic islet at 50 hpf (Figure 1B), parasympathetic extensions from the vagus nerve towards the pancreatic islet by 75 hpf (Figure 1C), and an extensive network of nerve fibers within the islet by 100 hpf (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Parasympathetic extensions from the vagus nerve towards the pancreatic islet are observed by 75 hpf.
source: Looking more closely, we first observed the migration of the vagus nerve near the pancreatic islet at 50 hpf (Figure 1B), parasympathetic extensions from the vagus nerve towards the pancreatic islet by 75 hpf (Figure 1C), and an extensive network of nerve fibers within the islet by 100 hpf (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: An extensive network of nerve fibers within the islet is observed by 100 hpf.
source: Looking more closely, we first observed the migration of the vagus nerve near the pancreatic islet at 50 hpf (Figure 1B), parasympathetic extensions from the vagus nerve towards the pancreatic islet by 75 hpf (Figure 1C), and an extensive network of nerve fibers within the islet by 100 hpf (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Both juvenile (25 dpf) and adult (1 year old) zebrafish display dense innervation networks within the endocrine pancreas.
source: Both juvenile (25 days post fertilization; dpf) and adult (1 year old) zebrafish display dense innervation networks within the endocrine pancreas (Figure 1E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1E-F.

claim: By 25 dpf, the celiac ganglion provides sympathetic innervation.
source: By 25 dpf, the celiac ganglion provides sympathetic innervation (Figure 1E), as previously described (Podlasz et al., 2016), and at this stage intra-pancreatic innervation between the primary and secondary islets is also present (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1E and a citation to prior literature.

claim: At 25 dpf, intra-pancreatic innervation between the primary and secondary islets is present.
source: By 25 dpf, the celiac ganglion provides sympathetic innervation (Figure 1E), as previously described (Podlasz et al., 2016), and at this stage intra-pancreatic innervation between the primary and secondary islets is also present (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The upregulation of elavl3 expression is a hallmark of post-mitotic neuron differentiation.
source: The upregulation of elavl3 expression is a hallmark of post-mitotic neuron differentiation (Dyer et al., 2014), and the elavl3 promoter activity can be used as a pan-neuronal reporter (Stevenson et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The elavl3 promoter activity can be used as a pan-neuronal reporter.
source: The upregulation of elavl3 expression is a hallmark of post-mitotic neuron differentiation (Dyer et al., 2014), and the elavl3 promoter activity can be used as a pan-neuronal reporter (Stevenson et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Post-mitotic neurons with elavl3 promoter activity were closely associated with the endocrine islet very early in development.
source: Post-mitotic neurons, with elavl3 promoter activity, were closely associated with the endocrine islet very early in development (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Starting around 28 hpf, neurons began to migrate toward the periphery of the endocrine cluster, and a subset of neurons detached from its anterior portion.
source: Starting around this time, neurons began to migrate toward the periphery of the endocrine cluster, and from 28 hpf a subset of neurons detached from its anterior portion (Figure 2A, Figure 2—videos 1–2).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2A and videos.

claim: The cells detaching from the endocrine cluster were not alpha, beta, or delta cells.
source: Whole mount immunostaining showed that the cells detaching from the endocrine cluster were not alpha, beta, or delta cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Detached neurons migrated rostrally, away from the endocrine cluster.
source: Subsequently, these neurons migrated rostrally, away from the endocrine cluster (Figure 2C, Figure 2—video 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2C and video.

claim: The vagus nerve extending from the nodose ganglion migrated caudally past the endocrine islet, and the vagus reporter signal overlapped with enteric nerves at 59–65 hpf.
source: Next, the vagus nerve extending from the nodose ganglion migrated caudally past the endocrine islet, and the vagus reporter signal overlapped with enteric nerves at 59–65 hpf (Figure 2D, Figure 2—video 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2D and video.

claim: As the detached neurons continued to migrate away from the endocrine cells, neurites extending toward the endocrine cluster could be observed.
source: As the detached neurons continued to migrate away from the endocrine cells, we could observe neurites extending toward the endocrine cluster (Figure 2E, Figure 2—video 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2E and video.

claim: At 80 hpf, immunostaining revealed the extension of neurites derived from elavl3-positive cells toward the islet.
source: At 80 hpf, immunostaining revealed the extension of neurites derived from elavl3-positive cells toward the islet (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Neurons also detached from the posterior end of the endocrine cluster and migrated caudally toward the developing secondary islets.
source: Interestingly, neurons also detached from the posterior end of the endocrine cluster and migrated caudally toward the developing secondary islets (Figure 2—video 7), while the other neurons stayed on the periphery of the primary islet.
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in video.

claim: Some neurons stayed on the periphery of the primary islet.
source: Interestingly, neurons also detached from the posterior end of the endocrine cluster and migrated caudally toward the developing secondary islets (Figure 2—video 7), while the other neurons stayed on the periphery of the primary islet.
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in video.

claim: Neurons that migrate caudally could be important for the formation of intra-pancreatic innervation.
source: These latter two neuronal populations could respectively be important for the formation of intra-pancreatic innervation (Figure 1E) and contribute to the peri-endocrine nerve plexus that has been reported in rodents (Ushiki and Watanabe, 1997).
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the observed migration patterns and comparison to rodent anatomy.

claim: Neurons that stay on the periphery could contribute to the peri-endocrine nerve plexus that has been reported in rodents.
source: These latter two neuronal populations could respectively be important for the formation of intra-pancreatic innervation (Figure 1E) and contribute to the peri-endocrine nerve plexus that has been reported in rodents (Ushiki and Watanabe, 1997).
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the observed migration patterns and comparison to rodent anatomy.

claim: High degree of variation in vagus innervation was observed, similar to what was observed for enteric innervation.
source: Due to the high degree of variation in vagus innervation, which was also observed for enteric innervation (Olsson et al., 2008), and the slight developmental delay that occurs during the time-lapse imaging of anesthetized zebrafish, we observed variability in the exact developmental timing of individual cellular events in different embryos (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations from time-lapse imaging and a citation to prior literature about enteric innervation variability.

claim: A slight developmental delay occurs during the time-lapse imaging of anesthetized zebrafish.
source: Due to the high degree of variation in vagus innervation, which was also observed for enteric innervation (Olsson et al., 2008), and the slight developmental delay that occurs during the time-lapse imaging of anesthetized zebrafish, we observed variability in the exact developmental timing of individual cellular events in different embryos (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is an observation about the experimental method.

claim: Variability in the exact developmental timing of individual cellular events was observed in different embryos.
source: Due to the high degree of variation in vagus innervation, which was also observed for enteric innervation (Olsson et al., 2008), and the slight developmental delay that occurs during the time-lapse imaging of anesthetized zebrafish, we observed variability in the exact developmental timing of individual cellular events in different embryos (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The order of the cellular events was always the same despite variability in timing.
source: Nonetheless, the order of the cellular events was always the same and in combination with the immunostaining data, it allows us to propose a model for the initial establishment of parasympathetic innervation (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data and is used to justify the proposed model.

claim: A neural crest origin for pancreatic nerves has been suggested from lineage tracing and knockout studies in mouse.
source: A neural crest origin for pancreatic nerves has been suggested from lineage tracing and knockout studies in mouse (Plank et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: A population of neural-crest-derived cells expressing the elavl3 promoter was found in association with the endocrine islet at 35 hpf.
source: Using lineage tracing with Tg(sox10:CreERT2, myl7:GFP); Tg(ubb:loxP-CFP-loxP-nuc-mCherry) zebrafish upon tamoxifen treatment from 16 to 24 hpf (when the neural crest population reaches its peak) (Mongera et al., 2013), we found a population of neural-crest-derived cells expressing the elavl3 promoter in association with the endocrine islet at 35 hpf (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 3A, B.

claim: The neural crest population reaches its peak between 16 to 24 hpf.
source: Using lineage tracing with Tg(sox10:CreERT2, myl7:GFP); Tg(ubb:loxP-CFP-loxP-nuc-mCherry) zebrafish upon tamoxifen treatment from 16 to 24 hpf (when the neural crest population reaches its peak) (Mongera et al., 2013), we found a population of neural-crest-derived cells expressing the elavl3 promoter in association with the endocrine islet at 35 hpf (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Live imaging revealed the migration of neural-crest-derived cells toward the islet before 27 hpf, their contact with the islet, and subsequently their migrating away from the islet.
source: Live imaging of Tg(sox10:GAL4); Tg(UAS:GFP); Tg(sst2:RFP) zebrafish revealed the migration of neural-crest-derived cells toward the islet before 27 hpf, their contact with the islet, and subsequently their migrating away from the islet (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Immunostaining showed that the cells migrating away from the islet were not beta or delta cells.
source: Immunostaining showed that the cells migrating away from the islet were not beta or delta cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: elavl3 promoter activity was observed in a subpopulation of endocrine cells.
source: Although elavl3 promoter activity was observed in a subpopulation of endocrine cells (Figure 2B), our data suggest that they do not contribute to the subset of cells migrating away from the islet.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Endocrine cells with elavl3 promoter activity do not contribute to the subset of cells migrating away from the islet.
source: Although elavl3 promoter activity was observed in a subpopulation of endocrine cells (Figure 2B), our data suggest that they do not contribute to the subset of cells migrating away from the islet.
evidence: This is an inference based on the immunostaining data.

claim: Immunostaining for HuC/HuD was not observed in the subpopulation of neural-crest-derived cells migrating away from the islet.
source: Interestingly, we also did not observe immunostaining for HuC/HuD in this subpopulation of neural-crest-derived cells (Figure 3E), suggesting that these cells are not yet fully mature neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The neural-crest-derived cells migrating away from the islet are not yet fully mature neurons.
source: Interestingly, we also did not observe immunostaining for HuC/HuD in this subpopulation of neural-crest-derived cells (Figure 3E), suggesting that these cells are not yet fully mature neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of HuC/HuD immunostaining.

claim: Nerve extensions toward the primary islet at 90 and 120 hpf were derived from cells that were once positive for sox10 promoter activity.
source: We found that nerve extensions toward the primary islet at 90 and 120 hpf were indeed derived from cells that were once positive for sox10 promoter activity (Figure 4C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 4C-E.

claim: sox10-derived cells remained on the periphery of the primary islet.
source: We also observed sox10-derived cells that remained on the periphery of the primary islet (Figure 4C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 4C-E.

claim: The decrease in the number of sox10-derived cells in between the vagus nerve and pancreatic islet when comparing 90 to 120 hpf suggests that these cells are migrating toward the vagus nerve.
source: The decrease in the number of sox10-derived cells in between the vagus nerve and pancreatic islet when comparing 90 to 120 hpf suggests that these cells are migrating toward the vagus nerve (Figure 4C–E).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed decrease in cell numbers between two time points.

claim: sox10 mutants exhibit a severe depletion in neural crest cells.
source: Additionally, immunostaining of sox10 mutants, which exhibit a severe depletion in neural crest cells (Dutton et al., 2001), revealed a complete absence of pancreatic innervation even though the vagus nerve extension was present (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature and immunostaining data.

claim: sox10 mutants revealed a complete absence of pancreatic innervation even though the vagus nerve extension was present.
source: Additionally, immunostaining of sox10 mutants, which exhibit a severe depletion in neural crest cells (Dutton et al., 2001), revealed a complete absence of pancreatic innervation even though the vagus nerve extension was present (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The data agree with the neural crest origin of pancreatic innervation that has been reported in rodents.
source: Overall, these data agree with the neural crest origin of pancreatic innervation that has been reported in rodents (Plank et al., 2011; Nekrep et al., 2008; Muñoz-Bravo et al., 2013; Kozlova and Jansson, 2009; Jiang et al., 2003; Young and Newgreen, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data from the manuscript and citations to prior literature.

claim: cloche mutants lack most endothelial cells.
source: By utilizing cloche mutants, which lack most endothelial cells (Stainier et al., 1995; Liao et al., 1997; Reischauer et al., 2016) including those endothelial cells that give rise to the pancreatic vasculature (Field et al., 2003), we wanted to examine whether blood vessels were crucial for islet innervation (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: cloche mutants lack endothelial cells that give rise to the pancreatic vasculature.
source: By utilizing cloche mutants, which lack most endothelial cells (Stainier et al., 1995; Liao et al., 1997; Reischauer et al., 2016) including those endothelial cells that give rise to the pancreatic vasculature (Field et al., 2003), we wanted to examine whether blood vessels were crucial for islet innervation (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: cloche mutants display fairly severe defects.
source: Even though cloche mutants display fairly severe defects (Figure 5B–D) and the vasculature was completely absent throughout the gastrointestinal system, as visualized by Tg(kdrl:GFP) expression, by 80 hpf both the right and left vagus nerve extensions could be observed in wild-type and mutant fish (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B-D.

claim: The vasculature was completely absent throughout the gastrointestinal system in cloche mutants.
source: Even though cloche mutants display fairly severe defects (Figure 5B–D) and the vasculature was completely absent throughout the gastrointestinal system, as visualized by Tg(kdrl:GFP) expression, by 80 hpf both the right and left vagus nerve extensions could be observed in wild-type and mutant fish (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5E-F.

claim: By 80 hpf both the right and left vagus nerve extensions could be observed in wild-type and cloche mutant fish.
source: Even though cloche mutants display fairly severe defects (Figure 5B–D) and the vasculature was completely absent throughout the gastrointestinal system, as visualized by Tg(kdrl:GFP) expression, by 80 hpf both the right and left vagus nerve extensions could be observed in wild-type and mutant fish (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5E-F.

claim: Extensive innervation of the pancreatic islet, comparable to that in wild-type, was observed in cloche mutants.
source: Interestingly, extensive innervation of the pancreatic islet, comparable to that in wild-type, was also observed in cloche mutants (Figure 5G–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 5G-I.

claim: A dense network of nerves could still be observed in the pancreatic islet at 4 dpf in cloche mutants.
source: A dense network of nerves could still be observed in the pancreatic islet at 4 dpf (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting that this initial stage of islet innervation and its expansion does not require signaling from endothelial cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The initial stage of islet innervation and its expansion does not require signaling from endothelial cells.
source: A dense network of nerves could still be observed in the pancreatic islet at 4 dpf (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting that this initial stage of islet innervation and its expansion does not require signaling from endothelial cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that innervation is normal in cloche mutants lacking endothelial cells.

claim: Maintenance of nerve density likely requires vascular supply.
source: Thus, although it is likely that maintenance of nerve density requires vascular supply (Reinert et al., 2014), our studies indicate that the presence of a vascular network is not crucial for the establishment of innervation.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on a citation to prior literature and the authors' interpretation.

claim: The presence of a vascular network is not crucial for the establishment of innervation.
source: Thus, although it is likely that maintenance of nerve density requires vascular supply (Reinert et al., 2014), our studies indicate that the presence of a vascular network is not crucial for the establishment of innervation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data from cloche mutants.

claim: Targeted ablation of the detached cluster of neurons resulted in a significant reduction in innervation density compared to mock ablated controls.
source: In comparison to the mock ablated controls, where cells immediately adjacent to the leading front of the detached neurons were targeted with the same laser intensity (Figure 6C), there was a significant reduction in innervation density upon ablation of the detached cluster of neurons (Figure 6F–G), while extension of the vagus nerve and enteric innervation appeared unaffected (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by two-photon ablation experiments and quantification data shown in Figure 6C, F-G.

claim: Extension of the vagus nerve and enteric innervation appeared unaffected by targeted ablation of detached neurons.
source: In comparison to the mock ablated controls, where cells immediately adjacent to the leading front of the detached neurons were targeted with the same laser intensity (Figure 6C), there was a significant reduction in innervation density upon ablation of the detached cluster of neurons (Figure 6F–G), while extension of the vagus nerve and enteric innervation appeared unaffected (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The absence of differences in size and gross morphology of the fish suggests that the decline in innervation density was not due to developmental delay.
source: The absence of differences in size and gross morphology of the fish suggests that this decline in innervation density was not due to developmental delay (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that fish morphology was normal.

claim: Immunostaining at 80 hpf revealed no significant differences in islet mass or beta cell numbers between the ablated fish and mock ablated controls.
source: Immunostaining at 80 hpf for Insulin and Somatostatin revealed no significant differences in islet mass or beta cell numbers between the ablated fish and mock ablated controls; however, a significant decrease in delta cell numbers was observed (Figure 6H–J), suggesting that early innervation is involved in establishing or maintaining the delta cell pool.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 6H-J.

claim: A significant decrease in delta cell numbers was observed in ablated fish compared to mock ablated controls.
source: Immunostaining at 80 hpf for Insulin and Somatostatin revealed no significant differences in islet mass or beta cell numbers between the ablated fish and mock ablated controls; however, a significant decrease in delta cell numbers was observed (Figure 6H–J), suggesting that early innervation is involved in establishing or maintaining the delta cell pool.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 6H-J.

claim: Early innervation is involved in establishing or maintaining the delta cell pool.
source: Immunostaining at 80 hpf for Insulin and Somatostatin revealed no significant differences in islet mass or beta cell numbers between the ablated fish and mock ablated controls; however, a significant decrease in delta cell numbers was observed (Figure 6H–J), suggesting that early innervation is involved in establishing or maintaining the delta cell pool.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that delta cell numbers decreased when innervation was reduced.

claim: Inhibition of neural activity did not result in developmental delay at 80 hpf.
source: Inhibition of neural activity did not result in developmental delay at 80 hpf (Figure 7B–C); however, a significant decrease in islet nerve density was observed even though the vagus nerve developed normally (Figure 7E–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological data shown in Figure 7B-C.

claim: A significant decrease in islet nerve density was observed upon inhibition of neural activity even though the vagus nerve developed normally.
source: Inhibition of neural activity did not result in developmental delay at 80 hpf (Figure 7B–C); however, a significant decrease in islet nerve density was observed even though the vagus nerve developed normally (Figure 7E–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 7E-I.

claim: Analysis of immunostained fish with inhibited neural transmission revealed no differences in beta cell numbers but a significant decrease in delta cell numbers.
source: Similar to the targeted cell ablation approach, analysis of immunostained fish revealed no differences in beta cell numbers but a significant decrease in delta cell numbers (Figure 7K–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 7K-L.

claim: Delta cell hypertrophy was observed upon inhibition of neural transmission.
source: Interestingly, delta cell hypertrophy was observed (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), which could account for the significant increase in primary islet mass (Figure 7J).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: A significant increase in primary islet mass was observed upon inhibition of neural transmission.
source: Interestingly, delta cell hypertrophy was observed (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), which could account for the significant increase in primary islet mass (Figure 7J).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 7J.

claim: Delta cell hypertrophy could account for the significant increase in primary islet mass.
source: Interestingly, delta cell hypertrophy was observed (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), which could account for the significant increase in primary islet mass (Figure 7J).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of both delta cell hypertrophy and increased islet mass.

claim: Elevated free glucose levels were observed upon inhibition of neural transmission at 80 hpf.
source: Elevated free glucose levels were also observed upon inhibition of neural transmission at 80 hpf (Figure 7D), and they remained elevated at 5 dpf, similar to what we observed in sox10 mutants which lack neural crest cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by glucose measurement data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Elevated free glucose levels remained elevated at 5 dpf upon inhibition of neural transmission.
source: Elevated free glucose levels were also observed upon inhibition of neural transmission at 80 hpf (Figure 7D), and they remained elevated at 5 dpf, similar to what we observed in sox10 mutants which lack neural crest cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by glucose measurement data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Elevated free glucose levels were observed in sox10 mutants which lack neural crest cells.
source: Elevated free glucose levels were also observed upon inhibition of neural transmission at 80 hpf (Figure 7D), and they remained elevated at 5 dpf, similar to what we observed in sox10 mutants which lack neural crest cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by glucose measurement data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Global neuron ablation led to significant decreases in beta and delta cell numbers.
source: Upon treatment with metronidazole (MTZ, a pro-drug that is converted to a cytotoxic form in the presence of NTR) from 24 to 80 hpf to induce global neuronal ablation, we detected significant decreases in beta and delta cell numbers (Figure 7—figure supplement 3C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by genetic ablation experiments and quantification data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3C-D.

claim: The early establishment of parasympathetic innervation requires the presence of neurons that are initially associated with the endocrine pancreas.
source: Overall, our data suggest that the early establishment of parasympathetic innervation requires the presence of neurons that are initially associated with the endocrine pancreas as well as active neural transmission.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ablation experiments showing reduced innervation when these neurons are removed.

claim: The early establishment of parasympathetic innervation requires active neural transmission.
source: Overall, our data suggest that the early establishment of parasympathetic innervation requires the presence of neurons that are initially associated with the endocrine pancreas as well as active neural transmission.
evidence: This is an inference based on the botulinum toxin experiments showing reduced innervation when neural transmission is blocked.

claim: Significant changes in pancreatic delta cell mass were observed upon decreased islet nerve density.
source: Notably, significant changes in pancreatic delta cell mass were observed upon decreased islet nerve density.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the ablation and botulinum toxin experiments.

claim: A dense supply of nerve fibers could be observed within the endocrine pancreas of developing and adult zebrafish, similar to what has been reported in rodents.
source: Similar to what has been reported in rodents (Hsueh et al., 2017; Tang et al., 2018), a dense supply of nerve fibers could be observed within the endocrine pancreas of developing and adult zebrafish.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data from the manuscript and citations to prior literature.

claim: Parasympathetic innervation predominates prior to 5 dpf.
source: Parasympathetic innervation predominates prior to 5 dpf, but by 25 dpf, sympathetic innervation extending from the celiac ganglia was also detected.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data from the manuscript.

claim: By 25 dpf, sympathetic innervation extending from the celiac ganglia was detected.
source: Parasympathetic innervation predominates prior to 5 dpf, but by 25 dpf, sympathetic innervation extending from the celiac ganglia was also detected.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data from the manuscript.

claim: Galaninergic nerves have been previously identified in the zebrafish pancreas.
source: Galaninergic nerves have been previously identified in the zebrafish pancreas (Podlasz et al., 2016), and as in non-human primates these nerves are parasympathetic (Verchere et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In non-human primates, galaninergic nerves are parasympathetic.
source: Galaninergic nerves have been previously identified in the zebrafish pancreas (Podlasz et al., 2016), and as in non-human primates these nerves are parasympathetic (Verchere et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The neurons present on the periphery of the islet could give rise to the peri-endocrine nerve plexus which has been observed in rodents.
source: The neurons present on the periphery of the islet as revealed in our studies could give rise to the peri-endocrine nerve plexus which has been observed in rodents (Tang et al., 2014; Ushiki and Watanabe, 1997).
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the observed location of neurons and comparison to rodent anatomy.

claim: This is the first report of the physical proximity of neurons and their targets prior to the migration of these neurons away from the developing target organ and eventual organ innervation.
source: To our knowledge, ours is the first report of the physical proximity of neurons and their targets prior to the migration of these neurons away from the developing target organ and eventual organ innervation.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: The uncovered sequence of events is reminiscent of the pioneer neuron model first proposed over a century ago.
source: The uncovered sequence of events is reminiscent of the pioneer neuron model first proposed over a century ago and which has been observed in various model systems, including Drosophila (Sánchez-Soriano and Prokop, 2005; Lin et al., 1995; Jacobs and Goodman, 1989), zebrafish (Hoijman et al., 2017; Wanner and Prince, 2013), and mouse (Morante-Oria et al., 2003; Stainier and Gilbert, 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature about the pioneer neuron model.

claim: A key difference between what was observed and the classical pioneer neuron model is that in the zebrafish pancreas these neurons are not migrating toward the target organ.
source: However, a key difference between what we observed and the classical model is that in the zebrafish pancreas these neurons are not migrating toward the target organ where they provide instructional cues for neuronal specification (Hoijman et al., 2017) or lay down axon tracks for the following neurons (Wanner and Prince, 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed migration pattern and comparison to the classical model.

claim: The neurons migrate away from the target organ while maintaining contact via neural extensions, which may subsequently provide tracks for other neurons to migrate along to reach their targets.
source: Instead, we observed the migration of these neurons away from the target organ while maintaining contact via neural extensions, which may subsequently provide tracks for other neurons to migrate along to reach their targets.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the observed migration pattern and neural extensions.

claim: The diminished innervation density following targeted ablation revealed the crucial role of neurons that initially associate with the endocrine cells.
source: Indeed, the diminished innervation density following their targeted ablation revealed the crucial role of these neurons that initially associate with the endocrine cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ablation experiments.

claim: Targeted ablation of neurons on the periphery of the islet at later stages should help decipher their role.
source: Targeted ablation of these neurons at later stages should help decipher their role.
evidence: This is a speculation about future experiments.

claim: A specific effect on delta cell mass was observed upon diminished nerve density.
source: Interestingly, a specific effect on delta cell mass was observed upon diminished nerve density.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the ablation experiments.

claim: Global neural inhibition led to a decline in delta cell mass.
source: Likewise, global neural inhibition and global neuron ablation also led to a decline in delta cell mass.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the botulinum toxin experiments.

claim: Global neuron ablation led to a decline in delta cell mass.
source: Likewise, global neural inhibition and global neuron ablation also led to a decline in delta cell mass.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the genetic ablation experiments.

claim: In the case of global neuron ablation, a decline in beta cell mass was also observed likely due to secondary effects from the extensive levels of neuronal cell death.
source: However, in the case of global neuron ablation, we also observed a decline in beta cell mass likely due to secondary effects from the extensive levels of neuronal cell death.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that beta cell mass decreased only in the global ablation condition.

claim: It is possible that delta cell loss could worsen the decline in innervation density given the potential role of Somatostatin signaling in mediating migration of developing neurons.
source: Given the potential role of Somatostatin signaling in mediating migration of developing neurons (Yacubova and Komuro, 2002), it is possible that delta cell loss could worsen the decline in innervation density.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on a citation to prior literature about Somatostatin signaling.

claim: The neural-crest-derived cells were not positive for Insulin, Glucagon, or Somatostatin staining at 90 hpf.
source: The neural-crest-derived cells were not positive for Insulin, Glucagon, or Somatostatin staining at 90 hpf (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Comparable neural density in the absence of vasculature indicates that it is dispensable for early pancreatic innervation.
source: Comparable neural density in the absence of vasculature indicates that it is dispensable for early pancreatic innervation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cloche mutant experiments showing normal innervation without vasculature.
